Tides
Tides are the rise and fall of the sea caused by the pull of the Moon and the Sun and by the turning of the Earth, and this series covers the ways they have been measured, explained and predicted, from the first tide tables written for harbour pilots to the global models used for shipping and flood defence today, together with the people who made them.

Ada Pellworth (4 March 1901 – 9 November 1968) was an English mathematician and hydrographer who devised the first practical method for predicting the tides of shallow estuaries.[1] Her tables were used by harbour authorities around the North Sea for more than forty years, and the argument she used to prove that her method converges became a standard tool in the study of slowly changing boundaries, well outside the field in which she first used it.

Born in Husum to an English father and a German mother, Pellworth grew up on the Wadden Sea coast, where the tide comes in across miles of flat sand faster than a person can walk. She studied mathematics at Newnham College, Cambridge, and stayed on to write a doctoral thesis on the stability of harmonic series, which was examined in 1927 and published, much revised, three years later.[2]

Early life and education

Family

Not to be confused with Ada Pellworth-Hale.

Pellworth's father was a surveyor for a shipping insurer, and his work took the family up and down the coast between Esbjerg and Emden. She later wrote that she learned arithmetic from his soundings, which he let her copy out in the evenings.[1]

She noticed before she was ten that the tide tables he carried were wrong by as much as an hour whenever the wind had been in the west for a week, and she kept a notebook of the errors, which survives among her papers and which she showed to her students for the rest of her life.

School

Main article: Husum Gymnasium

At the gymnasium in Husum she was the only girl in the mathematics class, and her teacher, who had studied under Felix Klein, lent her his own copies of the journals he read. When the family moved to England in 1916 she was placed a year below her age because her English was poor, and she spent that year, by her own account, reading the whole of the school library's shelf on navigation and ignoring everything else.

Notes

  1. ↑ Several sources give her year of birth as 1902, following the entry in the register of Newnham College, which was made when she arrived in England and gave her age on the day she was admitted rather than her date of birth. Her German birth certificate, which her nephew deposited with the college archive in 1974, settles the question in favour of 1901, and the college has since corrected its register, though the older date is still repeated in some of the biographical dictionaries that copied it.
